intro.sub: Twelve steps, thirteen landmarks, countless musical possibilities.
paras: An interval tells you how far apart two notes are. Hear one as a melody, play both notes together, or move one voice while another stays. The distance has a musical name—but what it feels like depends on the sounds, the moment and the listener.
These colors are **suggestions for remembering and painting**, not rules about what music must feel like. Pick the colors that fit your experience.

rows.name: Perfect unison
rows.role: Exact same pitch can reinforce a line, double a voice or create a single center. Two instruments on one note may still have contrasting timbres.

rows.name: Minor second
rows.role: Neighboring pitches can create close color or audible roughness depending on spectrum, register and dynamics. A melodic half-step can feel like a tiny lean.

rows.name: Major second
rows.role: An ordinary whole-step melody motion; together, the notes can form a spacious cluster or a suspended/accompaniment color.

rows.name: Minor third
rows.role: Important minor-triad building block, but also a characteristic melodic leap with many different expressive uses.

rows.name: Major third
rows.role: Part of major-triad identity and a widely recognizable dyad in Western tonal settings; changing its upper note transforms the shared sonority.

rows.name: Perfect fourth
rows.role: Useful for held drones, open voicings, melodic leaps and suspended combinations; its tonal stability depends on the bass and musical context.

rows.name: Tritone
rows.role: Exactly half an equal-tempered octave; often a striking contrasting color in tonal contexts, yet can feel intriguing or still in other textures.

rows.name: Perfect fifth
rows.role: An open structural frame in drones, open fifths, and melodic calls; simple ratios in just tuning often encourage strong fusion.

rows.name: Minor sixth
rows.role: A wide melodic gesture that can feel lyrical or dramatic; inversion of a major third, and a useful tension/color above sustained tones.

rows.name: Major sixth
rows.role: A singing melodic leap and soft extended-harmony color; inversion of a minor third.

rows.name: Minor seventh
rows.role: Appears in dominant/minor-seventh chords, melodic leaps, and modal/drone combinations that can hold an open edge.

rows.name: Major seventh
rows.role: Can feel delicate or restless when simultaneous; melodically an expressive near-octave leap. The B immediately below C5 often points upward in C-major context.

rows.name: Perfect octave
rows.role: Same letter/pitch class across a doubled-frequency relationship, often used to double a line or open up the register.

lesson2a.Learner heading: `Meet the intervals: a palette of musical distances`
lesson2a.Opening: Our first dyad is C and E. The interval between them is a **major third—four semitones**. When the top note moves to F, the same lower C now forms a **perfect fourth—five semitones**. Every interval has a name and a distance you can learn to recognize. Let's explore a small palette, then come back to the exact notes we're using today.
lesson2a.Default emphasis: IP-04 major third (starting pair), IP-05 perfect fourth (C+F), IP-02 major second (D+E as a non-C-root pair—**do not misleadingly imply all five example pairs begin on C**), IP-03 minor third (E+G and/or D+F). Preview IP-06 tritone as `Coming in Lesson 2B` without implying it is a required Lesson 2A interval. Keep the full 0–12 octave strip visible for browsing, but *open only these four focused cards by default*.
lesson2a.Critical distinction: The quick one-octave reference **anchors C4 for orientation**, but actual lesson dyads can begin on B3, D4, E4 etc. The interval's semitone distance does not change when both pitches are transposed by equal amounts. A minor third can be E4–G4 or D4–F4. The resource overlay must be able to calculate exact pitch pair and label that pair, rather than relabeling every example as `C–E♭`.
lesson2a.Context sentence: The same two pitches can sound very different when they're played one after another, held together, moved to another register, or placed above a different bass. An interval is a tool, not a fixed emotional instruction.
lesson2a.Shared tool controls: `Hear together`, `Hear one after another`, `Try a new register`, `Compare`, `Read more`, `Choose my own colors` (optional in-page mapping; do not imply persistence).
lesson2a.Artwork: existing Style B Quiet Paper grammar; preserve clean factual keyboard and note names; user may paint her own associations via the [Paint What You Hear](../../PAINT_WHAT_YOU_HEAR_STUDIO_V1.md) module. All emotional words are invitations. **Read every interval's deep chapter** in [DEEP_ATLAS_CONTENT_V1.md](DEEP_ATLAS_CONTENT_V1.md) for accurate musical context, melodic vs simultaneous difference and practical use.
